label: Outside witness
knownFor: A Roman historian whose Annals, his year-by-year history of Rome, tell how Nero put the blame for the fire of Rome on the Christians, and name Christus, that is, Christ, as put to death under Pontius Pilate.
shortDescription: Tacitus was a Roman historian who despised the Christians and named Christus, that is, Christ, as put to death under Pontius Pilate. In a few sentences, his Annals give the fullest account from outside the church of how the emperor Nero punished them after the great fire of Rome in 64.
datesNote: His own text gives no date. He wrote a generation or more after the great fire of Rome in 64. Tertullian says the fifth book of another of his histories began the account of the Jewish war, so that work came after the war
placeNote: Rome, after the great fire; Nero's gardens, where the Christians were put to death as a show; Judaea, where, Tacitus says, their religion began

keyWorks.title: Annals, Book 15, chapter 44
keyWorks.about: his year-by-year history of Rome. The one chapter the Library holds tells the prayers after the fire of Rome, Nero's blame and punishment of the Christians, and Christus put to death under Pilate. The part on the Christians runs to about 140 words of Latin, in six sentences

keyWorks.title: Histories
keyWorks.about: another of his histories, not held in the Library. Tertullian of Carthage cites it for what Tacitus said of the Jews: where they came from, a donkey's head, and the Roman general Pompey in the temple at Jerusalem

traces: About 400, Sulpicius Severus, a Christian writing a short history of the world, told the fire and the blame, and gave the same deaths in nearly Tacitus's own Latin words. He names no source, and he calls the dead innocent.

Later in the same history, Sulpicius calls the teaching of the Gnostics, found in Spain in his day, a deadly superstition. It was a secret teaching, he says, that came from the East and Egypt. His English translator and his Latin editor both point to Tacitus there, who used the same words, a deadly superstition, for the Christians' religion.
remembered: Tertullian of Carthage, defending the Christians about 200, answered Tacitus by name for his account of the Jews. In To the Nations he calls him "most loquacious in falsehood", the wordiest of liars.

Richard Hooker quoted the Latin of the chapter's lines on Nero's blame and on Christus. His point was that "in the estimation of the rest of the world even Christ Jesus himself was execrable", that is, hated.

Thierry Ruinart, a monk who died in 1709, answered Henry Dodwell, whose study published at Oxford in 1684 argued that very few Christians died for their faith in the early persecutions. Ruinart put Nero's persecution first, and wrote that Dodwell did not dare deny what Tacitus reports.
William Whiston, who translated Josephus, set the chapter's lines on Nero's blame and on Christ first among the ancient citations he gathered beside Josephus.

In 1876, Robert Roberts and Charles Bradlaugh, an atheist, debated in public whether the Bible is divine. Roberts quoted Tacitus with Pliny the Younger to show a great number of believers in Christ in the first century. Bradlaugh called the quotation "liable to impeachment", since the church historian Eusebius does not quote it, but would not go to "absolute denial".

uncertain: Tacitus does not say where he learned about Christus.

What Tacitus leaves open. He does not say what the Christians' shameful acts were, what the first ones arrested confessed, or who gave the order that people believed had set the fire. He names none of the dead.

Christus and the governor. The Latin says Christus was put to death "per procuratorem", by the procurator, the Roman governor. The 1876 English reads "at the hands of one of our procurators", and so adds "one of our".
The details of these deaths rest on Tacitus alone among the old sources the Library holds. Sulpicius Severus wrote more than three centuries later, in nearly Tacitus's words.

Sulpicius names no source. That he took the deaths from Tacitus rests on the wording. The held prints of Tacitus differ slightly at the crosses and the burning, so the words are nearly, not exactly, the same.

Sulpicius adds what Tacitus does not have: Nero away at Antium when the fire broke out, and Paul and Peter condemned at that time. He also says laws and edicts later made it unlawful to be a Christian.

Tertullian does not mention this chapter or the fire. His quarrel is with what Tacitus wrote of the Jews in his Histories, which the Library does not hold, so that account is known here only as Tertullian reports it.

What the verdict means. Tacitus says only that they were convicted less for setting the fire than for hatred of the human race. Thierry Ruinart took it to show that the Christians were judged worthy of death even before the fire.
Whether it is genuine. Among the writers the Library holds, only Charles Bradlaugh, in 1876, doubted it, and he would not deny it outright. Every other held writer uses it as Tacitus's.

The Latin is read differently in three places. The Library's note on its English says the Medicean manuscript, a handwritten copy of the Annals, reads chrestianos, corrected by a later hand. Mirbt and Schanz print Christianos. Mirbt prints convicti, convicted, where Ruinart reads conjuncti, joined. Mirbt has many nailed to crosses or burned with fire, where Ruinart has them nailed to crosses or set to be burned.
The Library holds one chapter of the Annals. Nothing in it shows what Tacitus says elsewhere.
The English is the translation standardly identified as Church and Brodribb's of 1876. The file itself names no translator.

briefReferences: Annals 15.44, in Halm's Latin as Mirbt prints it, with the 1876 English: the prayers and offerings after the fire, the talk that someone had ordered it, Nero's blame on people the crowd called Christians, Christus under Pilate, the deadly superstition breaking out again in Judaea and in Rome, the arrests and the verdict, the deaths in Nero's gardens, the chariot races, and the closing pity.
The Latin of the chapter, counted: the part on the Christians is about 140 words, in a few sentences. Among the old sources the Library holds, the details of these deaths rest on Tacitus alone.
When he wrote: his chapter gives no date, and Tertullian's report that his Histories told the Jewish war places that work after the war; a generation or more after the fire of 64.

Tertullian, Apology 16, in Oehler's Latin and the Ante-Nicene English, with Jerome on Carthage: Tacitus's account of the Jews in another of his histories, the donkey's head, the charge that he lied, and the general who found no image in the temple at Jerusalem.

Sulpicius Severus, Chronicle 2.29, in Halm's Latin and Alexander Roberts's English: the fire and the blame, the same deaths in nearly Tacitus's words, and the innocent; a short history of the world, down to the year 400.

timeline.when: After the great fire of Rome in 64
timeline.headline: Nero blames the Christians for the fire and puts them to death as a show
timeline.witness: Tacitus, Annals 15.44, written a generation or more later; the details of these deaths rest on him alone

lines.text: A great fire at Rome. Tacitus's chapter opens after it.
lines.note: The chapter gives no year; 64 is the generally accepted year.

lines.text: Rome turns to prayers and offerings to the gods.
Nothing, not human effort, not the emperor's gifts, not the offerings, ends the shameful talk that the fire was set on an order. Tacitus reports the belief and does not say who gave the order.

To kill the rumor, Nero puts forward as the guilty people hated for their shameful acts, whom the common crowd calls Christians, and punishes them with the most refined cruelty. Tacitus does not say what the shameful acts were.
Tacitus explains the name: Christus, that is, Christ, was put to death in the reign of the emperor Tiberius by the governor Pontius Pilate. He names no source for it.

He calls their religion a deadly superstition, which was held back for a moment but broke out again, in Judaea, where the evil began, and in Rome itself. Everything horrible or shameful, he says, flows into Rome from everywhere and finds a following.

First those who confessed are seized. Then, on their information, a huge number are convicted, less, he says, for setting the fire than for hatred of the human race. He names none of them, and does not say what the first ones confessed.

Mockery is added to their deaths. Some, covered in the skins of animals, are torn apart by dogs. Many are nailed to crosses or burned, and when daylight fails, others are set alight to light the night.
Nero offers his own gardens for the show. He also puts on chariot races, mixing with the crowd dressed as a charioteer, or standing in a chariot himself.

Pity rises, Tacitus writes, even for the guilty, who had earned the harshest punishment as a warning, since they seem to die not for the public good but for one man's cruelty. He still calls them guilty, and names no one who felt the pity.

lines.note: The Histories are not held in the Library.

lines.text: Tacitus tells Nero's punishment of the Christians in the Annals, his year-by-year history of Rome. His own text gives no date.

timeline.headline: Tertullian answers Tacitus by name, about the Jews
timeline.witness: Tertullian of Carthage, a Christian, in his Apology, his defense of the Christians

lines.text: Tacitus's account of the Jews, Tertullian says, started the tale that the Christians worship a donkey's head. Tacitus wrote that the Jews, dying of thirst in the desert, followed wild asses to water and honored the animal's head. People then took it that the Christians, close to the Jews in religion, worshiped the same.
lines.note: Jerome places Tertullian at Carthage under the emperors Severus and Antoninus Caracalla, cic/texts/anf03_tertullian.xml lines 620-624.

lines.text: Tertullian calls Tacitus a liar, and a wordy one, and points to his own words against him: the Roman general Pompey, who took Jerusalem, went into the temple and found no image there. If the Jews worshiped an image, Tertullian says, the temple was the very place it would be shown.
In To the Nations, another of his books, Tertullian makes the same answer about Pompey and the temple.
lines.reference: Tertullian, To the Nations 1.11, cic/texts/tertullian_opera-pars1-lat_reifferscheid-wissowa-csel20.txt lines 4914-4921; cic/texts/anf03_tertullian.xml lines 10090-10098

timeline.headline: Sulpicius Severus retells the deaths and calls the dead innocent
timeline.witness: Sulpicius Severus, a Christian, in his short history of the world down to the year 400

lines.text: Sulpicius tells the fire, with Nero away at Antium. People blamed the emperor, believing he sought the glory of building a new city, and Nero could not escape the charge that he had ordered the fire.
lines.note: Nero at Antium is Sulpicius's, not in the chapter of Tacitus the Library holds.

lines.text: Nero turned the blame onto the Christians, Sulpicius writes, and the cruelest tortures were used on the innocent. He gives the same deaths in nearly Tacitus's own Latin words, and names no source.
He adds that laws and edicts later made it unlawful to be a Christian, and that Paul and Peter were condemned at that time.
Later in the same history, he calls the teaching of the Gnostics, found in Spain in his day, a deadly superstition, the words Tacitus used for the Christians' religion.
lines.note: The echo of Tacitus is pointed out by his English translator and his Latin editor.

timeline.headline: A public debate, and the one held doubter
timeline.witness: The shorthand report of the debate, published by Robert Roberts

lines.text: In a six-night public debate at Leicester and Birmingham on whether the Bible is divine, Robert Roberts quotes Tacitus. With a letter of Pliny the Younger to the emperor Trajan, he uses it to show a great number of believers in Christ in the first century.
lines.reference: Is the Bible Divine?, cic/texts/roberts-bradlaugh_is-the-bible-divine-six-nights-discussion_1876.txt title and lines 2562-2569, 2620-2634

lines.text: Charles Bradlaugh, who calls himself an atheist, answers that the quotation from Tacitus is open to challenge, since Eusebius, the church historian, does not quote it. He will not go so far as to deny it outright.
lines.note: Eusebius's Church History gives Nero as the first persecutor from Tertullian, not from Tacitus, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 13834-13842.

lines.text: Roberts answers by reading out the historian Gibbon, who wrote that the most skeptical must respect the truth of the fact and the soundness of the passage.
